Nvidia’s $500B financing platforms, CME’s announcement of compute futures referencing Silicon Data indices, and our Series A all landed within days of each other. The timing is revealing.

As the industry moves from the training era into the inference era, compute is becoming a core production input. Post-trained open models, surging inference demand, and deeper enterprise adoption are arriving together. Inference compute is also becoming more fungible.

AI scaling is increasingly a capital problem rather than a pure technology problem: how the buildout gets financed, and who bears which risks. These are questions traditional capital markets are well equipped to answer, especially as inference income stabilizes and data centers begin to resemble more conventional capital assets.

These cash-settled futures give providers and buyers tools to manage that cost volatility the same way oil and crop futures helped those industries plan and expand with greater confidence. They are only the beginning. Rising fungibility will eventually open the door to physically settled instruments as well.

BREAKING: President Trump's capital gains tax cut discussions include "indexing" capital gains for inflation BEFORE taxes are calculated.

This would mean that taxes would be applied on gains adjusted for inflation.

For example, if you purchased a stock for $100,000 and sold it 5 years later for $200,000.

Under the current system, you would owe capital gains taxes on the full $100,000 gain.

But, if cumulative inflation over those 5 years was 20%, your inflation-adjusted cost basis would rise to $120,000.

This means you would only owe capital gains taxes on the $80,000 REAL gain, rather than the $100,000 nominal gain.

Trump has also suggested exemptions for sales of homes worth $2 million or less from capital gains taxes.

We expect more details soon.

🇺🇸 Nearly 13% of credit card balances are now more than 90 days delinquent, close to levels seen around the Global Financial Crisis. However, once you dig into the data, the picture is much more nuanced as the US consumer is under pressure, especially at the lower end, but we are still far from a genuine credit crisis.

💳 The key point is precisely about credit cards as that 12.8% figure measures the stock of distressed debt, which includes old balances that banks have already charged off but that can remain on consumers’ credit reports for a long time. The NY Fed shows that changes in reporting practices explain a significant part of the rise seen over the past several quarters.

⚠️ To understand whether conditions are actually deteriorating right now, it makes more sense to look at the flow of new balances becoming seriously delinquent, and there, the picture is far less dramatic. The rate is around 7% and virtually unchanged from a year ago. An elevated rate, of course, but it suggests that the sharp deterioration seen between 2022 and 2024 has broadly plateaued. We are also still well below the roughly 11% reached during the financial crisis.

🚙 The area where I am more cautious is auto credit as balances continue to rise, originations are picking up, the average credit quality of new borrowers has weakened slightly, and delinquencies remain elevated, particularly among 18-29 year-olds, where serious delinquency rates are approaching 5%. The US consumer is not uniformly weak and the economy is increasingly two-speed. A homeowner who refinanced a mortgage at 3% in 2021, owns financial assets and benefited from rising house prices is in a completely different position from a young renter financing a car at 9% and carrying credit card debt at more than 20%.

➡️ My takeaway is fairly straightforward, the US consumer is weakened but not breaking. Some groups are clearly under significant pressure but credit deterioration no longer appears to be accelerating and there is still no evidence of a systemic accident. What I would watch from here is the combination of rising unemployment with renewed acceleration in credit card and auto delinquencies, and tighter bank lending standards.

➡ If all three start moving in the wrong direction at the same time, the story becomes much more concerning.

*Link: https://t.co/Fa1NRNDjzl

Rather than one-and-done off of one year. 

This is a stark contrast to some other sectors where growth is likely to decelerate after maybe 1 year of triple digit Y/Y revenue growth.

different math for renters, but the baseline facts are the same

$CRWV +14% AH

Pricing power, reaccelerating bookings, and a residual value surprise ⬇️

>Rev $2.6B (+112% YoY, +24% QoQ), adj op income ~40% above high end of guide. Raised full-year rev guidance by $400M vs the $15M beat.

>Margins inflecting: adj op margin 1% in Q1, 5% in Q2, low-teens targeted Q4. Revenue + pricing scaling at least as fast debt load as deployments mature.

>July price hike ~25% across all SKUs, output inflation outpacing input costs

>New contract contribution margins 5-10pts above recent qtrs, led by Vera Rubin. We est. 65-70% contribution on new cloud, 80%+ on inference recontracts

>Backlog net add was modest in qtr (+$5B to $105B), but +$25B of fresh Q3 commitments since July 1 signals reacceleration

>Residual value: 2020-vintage GPUs still contracting 3+ years forward at attractive rates

>Recontracting not in base underwriting, every renewal is pure IRR upside

>Inference emerging as natural second life for older fleet coming off term contracts

>Inference ARR grew ~100x in a single quarter, targeting $250M by YE

>Active power 1.0 GW entering Q1, 1.5 GW exiting Q2, guided 1.85 GW by YE (up from 1.7GW). June alone added 300 MW, more than any prior full quarter in company history, with another 500MW contracted since qtr close

>CapEx guide raised again (by 11%), two qtrs running, demand signal and higher component costs

What the (raised) guidance implies:
2026 exit ARR of $18.5-19.5B implies Q4 revenue of $4.6-4.9B vs. Q3 guided at $3.45-3.6B. Q2 revs were back-end loaded but they have the $25B signed in July so off to a great start in 2H.

CRWV has beaten revenue guidance all 6 quarters public so as an industry investor I'd fade their full-year topline at your peril. Whether or not the stock represents good value here is an entirely other story and for another post.
